facts.t: Appears in 6.44% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive (1,532 paintings, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 989).
In our 23,781-painting archive it is more common than 91% of the named colors.
Peaks in the 1200s: found in 9.9% of the 142 paintings we have from then (14 paintings). Against the same museums' baseline that is 2.1x the expected rate.
Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color (38% of the 989 paintings, by lightness rank within each painting, so varnish cannot fake it).
Painted most often by John Singer Sargent (23 of 287 works here, 8% of them). No painter stands out against the museum baseline.

First seen in our archive in 1000 (cma-133068); the third-earliest painting is 1000, and the latest 2000 (1271 dated paintings, at least 2% of the canvas, as photographed). The archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first. That is 650 years before the name's earliest record in our sources (1650): the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of the pigment or dye.
Shares canvases with Veinous Blood Red and Mushroom brown more than chance (lift 6.1 and 5.6; n=108 and 89).
In printed English the word peaks in the 1880s and rose fastest in the 1880s (Google Books, adjective use only, which is the color sense).
